How I work

## Diagnosis before doctrine.

Sometimes the answer is a new system. Sometimes it is a targeted change to one that already works. The job is to identify the constraint, make the proportionate intervention, and connect it to a commercial result.

1. **See where value is moving**

   Read the technology shift, the buyer behavior behind it, and the commercial consequence before choosing a playbook.
2. **Make the bet**

   Decide what must change, what should stay intact, and where the company can build an advantage early.
3. **Build the operating system**

   Form follows function. Positioning, people, process, product surfaces, pricing, channels, and measurement all take their shape from the commercial job, not from an org chart template.

The arc

I started carrying a personal quota, moved to running commercial organizations, and for the last decade I have owned revenue numbers at company scale. Nineteen years, four continents, four industries: Medtech, Adtech, Fintech and B2B SaaS.

The constant is not a playbook. It is starting with how customers choose, adopt and get value, and building the commercial system accordingly.

How the results happen

## Acquire the right customers. Help them win with your product. Make getting value easier.

The rule underneath it is one I have used since Amazon: bring a person in when automation and mass communication are not enough. Done well, the cost of serving a customer stops tracking the revenue they produce.

At Taboola it took the unit from about $130M to $500M without scaling the team at the same rate. At Rapyd it became automated merchant onboarding. At Lokalise it became being the answer a buyer's AI gives.

Helping customers win, and making value easier to get, are exactly what AI now does more cost-effectively. That is why the shift below is a commercial challenge, not just a technical one.

Current point of view

## The part of the customer journey your dashboards barely register is getting larger.

Customers have been getting further on their own for a decade: finding you, comparing you, connecting you, running the product, fixing it when it breaks. What is changing is who is doing it. Increasingly it is a machine, which raises one question: how far do your customers, and their AI, get without you?

**The serviceable line** is how far your customers, and increasingly their AI, get with your offering on their own. Past that point, either one of your people has to step in, or you lose revenue, often without seeing why: left out of an AI's answer, judged on a smaller version of what you offer, or quietly gone after the trial or the first bill. Move the line out, and you can win customers you used to walk away from, and stop the losses you never measured.

How far AI moves the line depends on two things, and neither works without the other: how far your buyers have gone in handing this work to AI, and how legible your offering is to a machine. And the line sits in a different place at each of the five questions a customer's AI asks, from whether it can find you at all to whether it can recover when something breaks.

The direction is clear: more of the buying journey and more of the customer experience is becoming AI-mediated, and go-to-market practices built for an entirely human journey will need re-tooling. How fast each market moves is still unproven, and that is what decides where to act first.

Hands-on

## I have done the work across Sales and Marketing, led the teams, built the systems, and now build the tools.

I can tell whether a commercial plan will hold because I have done most of the jobs inside it. I carried a bag before I managed anyone carrying one: face to face, phone, events, negotiations and closing. The same is true across most of the other functions I run: partner deals, account plans, media buying, positioning, and the copy that goes in front of a buyer, on a screen, in print or from a stage.

The same instinct runs through the technology. I have built websites across three decades as the tooling changed: **hand-written HTML**, then **WordPress**, now **AI-native**. I automated my home. After Lokalise I took that progression one step further and built a working AI operating system myself.

The operating test

## How much work one person could carry once AI was connected to real context and tools, and where that leverage stopped.

I built and run a working [personal AI operating system](https://etgarbonar.com/ai/) at the smallest useful scale: one operator, no team, real costs and real consequences. It works across family, household, travel, health, finance, research, writing and development.

The answer only became useful when I added the controls the demo layer skips: scoped permissions, human approval, watchdogs, canary tests, backups, incident logging and a written record of failures.

At Amazon, Taboola and Rapyd, I learned the same lesson while building self-service and PLG businesses: scale depended on how much of the journey a customer could complete without help. The same holds for AI. Progress stops when the customer or operator meets a sales gate, incomplete documentation or a missing API. That is the practical link between the system I built and the serviceable-line point of view above.
